vo.text: Every how-to video plays at the same speed, whether you keep up, or not.
Falls are the second-leading cause of unintentional injury death worldwide.
In one survey, three in four people didn't finish their home physical therapy exercises.
And most cardiac arrests outside hospital happen at home, where nobody is checking your form.
At least nine in ten deaf children are born to hearing parents.
And a video can't see whether your hands are right.
InStep is the video that waits for you.
Prop up your phone. It becomes the camera: an external camera, not the TV.
Pose tracking runs in the phone's browser. Only body points travel to the TV, never video.
At each key moment, the lesson pauses, and continues only when your pose is right.
It counts your reps, times your balance, and if you're stuck, a coach gives one short, kind tip.
Safety comes first: no balance work until a chair is beside you. And if the camera drops, the lesson stops.
The same engine teaches sign-language hand shapes, hand rehab, and CPR rhythm: practice only, not certification.
Kids act out a story. And two people can practise together.
A physiotherapist or teacher records a lesson once, on a phone.
InStep finds the still moments, suggests the steps, and publishes it to the TV.
Under the hood: an open lesson format called .istep,
one pure TypeScript gate engine, shared by the phone, the server and the TV,
and an open-source Vega player that any app can use.
InStep. The video that waits for you.
